name: sound-touch
why: Changes pitch and tempo independently, a real audio transform, though it is mostly a library and needs a use case to shine.

brief.what_it_is: SoundTouch is an open-source C++ audio processing library that changes the tempo, pitch, or playback rate of audio streams or files. It can also estimate stable beats-per-minute for a track. It takes audio in 16-bit integer or 32-bit float mono, stereo, or multi-channel formats and returns the processed audio. The source kit includes SoundStretch, an example command-line utility that processes .wav files.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says the library is 'intended for application developers writing sound processing tools that require tempo/pitch control functionality, or just for playing around with the sound effects.'
brief.how_it_works: The homepage explains the three modes: tempo (time stretch) changes speed without changing pitch, pitch changes key while keeping tempo, and playback rate changes both together, like a vinyl record played at a different RPM. It links to a tutorial on the theory of audio time and pitch scaling, but the homepage does not describe the algorithm itself.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install commands. It says the latest stable release is in the git repository (the page points to codeberg.org for source) and that compiled executables can be downloaded. The source builds with GNU C (gcc) or Visual C++ on Windows, macOS, Linux and other *nix systems, Raspberry Pi, Android and iOS. It has MMX and SSE optimizations for x86 and OpenMP for multi-core CPUs. It also ships C#, Java and C++ examples, and interface modules for C#, Pascal/Delphi and Java. The brew entry's executable is 'soundstretch'. No command lines were visible on the homepage, and I did not fetch the README or the SoundStretch page.
brief.standout: It is a real, mature time-stretch and pitch-shift engine with a small footprint: the page describes a single C++ class as the programming interface. Its real-time latency is quoted at about 100 ms, and the author claims CD-quality stereo can run in real time on a 133 MHz Pentium. Beats-per-minute estimation comes built in.
brief.status: Unknown from the homepage alone. The copyright line reads 'Copyright © Olli Parviainen 2001-2024', and the page refers to the 'latest stable release' in the git repository, but it gives no release date or commit date. The README and repository were not checked, so I could not confirm activity.
brief.caveats: Mostly a library, so it needs a use case; the only bundled app, SoundStretch, reads .wav files from the command line. Licensed under LGPL v2.1, with a commercial non-LGPL license available on request, and the page also mentions a royalty-free commercial license. Real-time use is limited by roughly 100 ms of stream latency. The brew entry's caveats field is empty.

Changes both tempo and pitch together as if a vinyl disc was played at different RPM rate.

entry.title: SoundTouch
entry.tldr: A small C++ audio library, with a bundled command-line tool called soundstretch, that changes tempo and pitch independently or together, and can estimate a track's BPM.
entry.deeper_look:
SoundTouch is an open-source library for changing the tempo, pitch, or playback rate of audio. It takes 16-bit integer or 32-bit float audio, mono, stereo, or multi-channel, and returns processed audio. The homepage says it is meant for developers who need tempo and pitch control, "or just for playing around with the sound effects." It also includes a beats-per-minute estimator.

The idea underneath is that speed and pitch are normally tied together. Speed up a record and it gets higher as well as faster. SoundTouch separates them into three modes. Tempo changes speed without changing pitch. Pitch changes key without changing speed. Playback rate changes both at once, "as if a vinyl disc was played at different RPM rate." Pulling those apart is time-stretching and pitch-shifting, a core technique in DJ tools, music practice apps, and audio editors.

The Homebrew formula installs soundstretch, the example command-line utility from the source kit. According to the homepage, it works on .wav files. The homepage links to a tutorial on the theory of audio time and pitch scaling, but it does not describe the algorithm itself, so that is where to dig further.

The library is small. The page describes a single C++ class as the programming interface, with examples and bindings for C#, Java, and Pascal/Delphi. It has been around since 2001.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage text and the options for changing tempo, pitch, and playback rate on a .wav file.

entry.whats_unique: It is a long-lived time-stretch and pitch-shift engine reduced to one C++ class, with BPM detection included. The author claims CD-quality stereo can run in real time on a 133 MHz Pentium.
entry.caveats: It is mostly a library, the bundled soundstretch tool only handles .wav files, and real-time use has about 100 ms of latency. I could not confirm recent activity from the homepage.
